Context: The team needs one controlled engineering environment from the start of M1, and the Master Project Brief section 9 mandates protected main, pull requests and two approvals.
Alternatives: A) Single repository with protected main and two required approvals. B) Single repository, trunk-based with direct commits and post-hoc review. C) Separate documentation and code repositories.
Decision: A - single controlled repository, protected main, pull request required, two approvals from members other than the author, no self-approval, linear history.
Rationale: It is the mandated control, it produces the review evidence the milestone assesses, and one repository keeps documentation and future code under a single traceable history.
Trade-offs: With three members, two approvals means unanimous consent from the other two; this is slower and creates a deadlock exposure.
Evidence / evidence required: Repository settings, branch protection rule, merged pull requests with two approvals
Downstream consequence: Every substantive artefact change from M1 onwards must pass through review, which is the evidence base for the individual defence.

Context: Three members must edit one controlled document concurrently under time pressure, and the review model requires that changes be reviewable.
Alternatives: A) Single shared .docx edited in a cloud office suite. B) Modular Markdown in the repository, compiled to a controlled document at baseline. C) One .docx per member, merged manually at the end.
Decision: B - the PED is authored as numbered Markdown sections in docs/PED/ and compiled to PED_v1.0.docx for submission and sign-off.
Rationale: Markdown produces line-level diffs, so a reviewer can see exactly what changed and approve a specific change. A binary .docx cannot be merged or meaningfully reviewed, and option C guarantees an integration crisis at the deadline.
Trade-offs: An extra compile-and-format step is needed before each baseline, and the submitted document must be regenerated rather than edited directly.
Evidence / evidence required: docs/PED/ section files, pull request diffs on individual sections
Downstream consequence: The compiled document is an output, never the source of truth. Any correction made directly in the .docx is lost at the next compile.

Context: Traceability across four milestones requires identifiers that remain stable as artefacts evolve.
Alternatives: A) Sequential numbering per artefact type with a fixed prefix. B) Hierarchical identifiers encoding the parent requirement. C) Descriptive slugs.
Decision: A - FR-nnn, NFR-nnn, AC-nnn, SH-nn, CF-nn, CN-nn, RSK-nn, DEC-nnn, FEC-nn, AS-nn, CHG-nnn, TST-nnn, DEF-nnn. Identifiers are never reused and never renumbered.
Rationale: Stable flat identifiers survive reprioritisation and deletion. Hierarchical identifiers break as soon as a requirement is split or moved, which is exactly what happens between M1 and M2.
Trade-offs: Identifiers carry no meaning, so a reader must consult the register rather than infer relationships from the number.
Evidence / evidence required: RTM, registers, commit messages and pull request titles referencing identifiers
Downstream consequence: Every later artefact - design, issue, test, defect, release note - attaches to these identifiers. Renumbering after baseline would break the RTM.

Context: All three members use AI assistants, and the Master Project Brief section 10 makes AI output non-authoritative and non-transferable in accountability.
Alternatives: A) Register material AI use with recorded verification, plus a declaration in the pull request. B) Register AI use only where code is generated. C) Prohibit AI use on controlled artefacts.
Decision: A - the AI Usage Register records material contributions with the verification actually performed, and the pull request template requires an AI declaration that the reviewer checks.
Rationale: The assessed risk is unverified content entering the baseline, which applies at least as much to requirements and risk text as to code. Prohibition would be unenforceable and would waste a permitted engineering aid.
Trade-offs: The register is only as good as the honesty of the entries, and maintaining it costs time on every substantive contribution.
Evidence / evidence required: AI Usage Register, pull request AI declaration field
Downstream consequence: Any member may be asked to explain any AI-assisted artefact, including one they did not author.

Context: Registers must be live artefacts that are reviewable in pull requests and presentable at the defence.
Alternatives: A) CSV in the repository as the source of truth, with a compiled workbook for presentation. B) Workbook only. C) Tables embedded in the PED only.
Decision: A - registers are held as CSV under docs/, and a compiled .xlsx is generated for presentation and submission.
Rationale: CSV changes appear as reviewable diffs, so a risk being downgraded or a requirement being edited is visible to reviewers. A workbook is opaque in review, and tables embedded only in the PED cannot be maintained between baselines.
Trade-offs: Two representations must be kept in step, and the workbook must be regenerated rather than edited.
Downstream consequence: The RTM and Risk Register remain diff-reviewable through M2 to M4, which is where most of their value lies.

Context: Requesters reporting security concerns want anonymity; management requires attributable accountability (CF-01).
Alternatives: A) Authenticated submission only. B) Anonymous submission permitted. C) Authenticated submission with an anonymity flag that hides identity from staff.
Decision: A - all submissions are authenticated in v1. Identity is protected by restricted visibility (NFR-012) rather than by absence of identity. A confidential channel is deferred (SCOPE-D-04).
Rationale: Accountability and audit are the core business need in the CivicConnect scenario, and an anonymous request cannot be clarified, updated or fed back on, which breaks FR-009 and FR-010. Option C requires a second authorisation model that the M1 scope cannot support.
Trade-offs: The reprisal concern raised by SH-01 is not fully resolved and remains open on the deferred register.
Downstream consequence: If a confidential channel is later accepted, the audit model and the notification model must both be revisited.

Context: Attachments would materially improve fault reporting, but introduce storage cost, malware exposure and a retention obligation.
Alternatives: A) Include attachments in v1. B) Defer pending platform and evidence. C) Exclude permanently.
Decision: DEFERRED - decision to be taken at M2 once the platform decision establishes actual free-tier storage limits.
Rationale: Committing now would bind the M2 platform choice to a storage requirement whose cost is unknown, which inverts the correct decision order.
Trade-offs: Fault reports remain text-only in the interim, which SH-02 may find limiting.
Evidence / evidence required: Evidence still required: free-tier object-storage limits of candidate platforms; frequency with which a photograph is genuinely needed; malware-scanning options at zero cost; retention rules for images containing personal data.
Downstream consequence: Affects persistence design, upload validation, security testing and operational cost from M2 onwards.

Decision area: Technology stack, architecture and deployment platform
Context: These are the most consequential technical decisions in the project and are explicitly outside the M1 boundary.
Decision: DEFERRED to M2, to be taken through a weighted decision matrix and an Architecture Decision Record supported by a measured proof of concept.
Rationale: The evidence required to choose well does not exist yet. Baselined requirements and NFRs are inputs to the decision, not outputs of it. Choosing a stack in M1 would be a preference exercise rather than an engineering decision, and the Master Project Brief makes technology selection an assessed decision.
Trade-offs: The team cannot begin construction, which compresses M2. Accepted deliberately.
Evidence / evidence required: Evidence still required: verified availability and compatibility on the Belgium Campus desktop platform; free-tier limits and cold-start behaviour of candidate hosts; an honest team capability audit; a small proof of concept exercising authentication, persistence and deployment.
Downstream consequence: Determines architecture, persistence, CI, deployment, operational cost and the achievability of NFR-001, NFR-002, NFR-010 and NFR-013.

Context: Scope must be reducible under schedule pressure without renegotiating every requirement.
Alternatives: A) MoSCoW. B) Numeric 1-5 priority. C) Ordered backlog only.
Decision: A - MoSCoW, with Must reserved for requirements without which the minimum business capabilities in Master Project Brief section 3 are not met.
Rationale: MoSCoW makes the contingency in RSK-12 executable: under pressure the team drops Could and Should items in a defined order rather than negotiating individually. A numeric scale invites everything to be rated 5.
Trade-offs: MoSCoW carries no ordering within a band, so sequencing still requires the backlog.
Downstream consequence: The Must set defines the minimum releasable product and the M3 scope-freeze contingency.

Decision area: Team Working Agreement and review service level
Context: The two-approval rule creates a deadlock exposure with three members (RSK-04).
Alternatives: A) 24-hour review turnaround with a fixed daily review window and small single-purpose pull requests. B) Review on demand. C) Batched weekly review.
Decision: A - documented in docs/governance/team-working-agreement.md and agreed by all three members.
Rationale: A fixed turnaround makes review latency predictable, and small pull requests make review cheap enough to actually perform properly. Batched review would concentrate risk immediately before the milestone.
Trade-offs: Requires daily engagement from all three members regardless of whose workstream is active.
Evidence / evidence required: Team Working Agreement, pull request timestamps showing review latency
Downstream consequence: Sets the collaboration cadence for all four milestones and is the first evidence of team accountability.

Decision area: Role model reduced to four roles
Context: The scenario implies a Coordinator role distinct from Management oversight (SH-03).
Alternatives: A) Four roles - Requester, Staff, Manager, Administrator. B) Five roles adding Coordinator.
Decision: A - the Coordinator responsibilities of SH-03 are served by the Manager role in v1.
Rationale: A fifth role multiplies the authorisation test matrix in NFR-004 for a separation of duty that no stakeholder has stated as a need. Scope discipline favours the smaller controlled model.
Trade-offs: If assignment volume grows, Managers carry coordination workload that a dedicated role would absorb; SH-03 needs are met functionally but not organisationally.
Downstream consequence: Adding a role after baseline changes the authorisation matrix, the test matrix and every screen that branches on role.

Context: Management wants reporting depth; staff want fast submission (CF-02).
Alternatives: A) Single-level controlled list. B) Two-level category and subcategory.
Decision: A - a single-level controlled list, administered under FR-023.
Rationale: A single level keeps the submission form to one selector, keeps FR-020 reporting reconcilable, and keeps the target resolution time in FR-021 attached to exactly one level. Two levels double the administration and create ambiguous parent-level reporting.
Trade-offs: Reporting granularity is limited to the top level, which SH-04 may find coarse once real volume exists.
Downstream consequence: Introducing a second level later requires data migration of existing requests and a change to every report.
